entries.title: Understanding and troubleshooting Android memory
entries.summary: Memory is a critical and finite resource on Android-powered devices. As an Android platform developer or OEM, understanding how memory works at every level---from the Java runtime down to the Linux kernel---is essential for building a performant and stable system.

entries.title: App code is memory
entries.summary: The code you write is itself a form of memory use. Every class, method, and string constant in your application must be loaded into RAM when it is executed. The larger your application's code base, the more memory it will consume just to exist.

entries.title: Bitmaps and memory
entries.summary: Bitmap objects are often the largest single contributors to an application's memory footprint. Whether it's app icons, notification images, or media content, inefficient bitmap handling can quickly lead to Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors and system-wide memory pressure.

entries.title: Fundamental concepts
entries.summary: To understand memory usage on Android, you must look at the system from several different perspectives, ranging from high-level Java objects down to low-level kernel pages.

entries.title: Analyzing Java memory
entries.summary: Java and Kotlin applications manage memory through a garbage-collected heap. When objects are no longer reachable, the garbage collector (GC) eventually reclaims their space. Memory leaks occur when objects that are no longer needed are still held by "GC roots," preventing them from being reclaimed.

entries.title: Service bindings and process states
entries.summary: App processes on Android do not exist in isolation. Applications often rely on services provided by other applications or the system itself. When one process connects to another via a **Service Binding**, it creates a dependency that has a profound impact on how the Android framework manages memory.

entries.title: Threads and memory
entries.summary: Every time your application creates a new thread, the operating system must allocate memory to support it. While threads are generally considered "lightweight" compared to full processes, their memory cost is not zero. Leaking threads is a very common way to leak memory on Android.

entries.title: Where to hoist state

entries.title: Define and query one-to-many relationships
entries.summary: A *one-to-many relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to zero or more instances of the child entity, but each instance of the child entity can only correspond to exactly one instance of the parent entity.

entries.title: Define and query one-to-one relationships
entries.summary: A *one-to-one relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to exactly one instance of the child entity, and the reverse is also true.

entries.summary: Notifications on watches use the same APIs and have the same structure as notifications on phones.

entries.title: Bridging options for notifications
entries.summary: By default, the system *bridges*, or shares, notifications from a phone app to any paired watches. If you build a watch app and your app also exists on a paired phone, users might receive duplicate notifications---one that the phone app generates and bridges, and one that the watch app generates. entries.summary: Wear OS devices are often used for long-running experiences, such as tracking a workout. These experiences may also provide important information that the user cares about and needs quick access to.

entries.title: Develop tiles for different screen sizes

entries.title: Physical buttons

entries.title: Save power using ambient mode requirements
entries.summary: All watch faces should have not only an interactive mode, but also ambient mode. The Wear OS App Quality guidelines specify that only [15% of pixels are illuminated in ambient mode](https://developer.android.com/docs/quality-guidelines/wear-app-quality#wff).

entries.title: Represent the time

entries.title: Dynamically change element appearance
entries.summary: You may want to change the appearance of parts of the watch face, for example, change the position, size, visibility, often in response to [input data sources](https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/wff/common/attributes/source-type) such as the time of day or the accelerometer.

entries.title: Dynamically change element content
entries.summary: While `Transform` lets you change the appearance of elements or groups of elements, there might be occasions where you want to switch between a list of behaviors based on some condition. This is analogous to a `switch` statement or `if...else` statement in other languages.

entries.title: Create animated images
entries.summary: In addition to static images on the watch face, animated images can bring a further dimension to the user experience.

entries.title: Weather data in the Watch Face Format
entries.summary: Since version 2, the Watch Face Format includes support for weather data. This data covers a range of metrics and timeframes, from the current conditions to hourly and daily forecasts.

entries.title: Define and query many-to-many relationships
entries.summary: A *many-to-many relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to zero or more instances of the child entity, and the reverse is also true.

entries.title: Define and query nested relationships
entries.summary: Sometimes, you might need to query a set of three or more tables that are all related to each other. In that case, you define *nested relationships* between the tables.

entries.title: Define and query one-to-many relationships
entries.summary: A *one-to-many relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to zero or more instances of the child entity, but each instance of the child entity can only correspond to exactly one instance of the parent entity.

entries.title: Define and query one-to-one relationships
entries.summary: A *one-to-one relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to exactly one instance of the child entity, and the reverse is also true.

entries.summary: [Complications](https://developer.android.com/design/ui/wear/guides/surfaces/complications) are a feature of both physical and smartwatch watch faces that show additional information. Typically the user selects what information is shown in a complication.

entries.title: Apply masks, blend effects, and tints
entries.summary: The `Group` and `Part*` elements also provide `tintColor, renderMode` and `blendMode` attributes which are powerful ways of adjusting the appearance of sections of your watch face.

entries.title: Arrange elements into groups
entries.summary: Groups allow you to separate your watch face design into a logical structure.

entries.title: Work with images
entries.summary: Using images in your watch face can really help bring it to life, from a full-screen background image to individual detail images to add interest.

entries.title: Optimize memory usage for your watch face

entries.title: Personalize with photos
entries.summary: **Note**: This feature is available on version 4 and higher of Watch Face Format.

entries.title: Define user configurations
entries.summary: `UserConfigurations` let you create options that the user can choose between. You can adjust the appearance of watch face elements based on the chosen values.

entries.title: Work with text
entries.summary: For digital clocks, you should aim to use `DigitalClock` where possible. For all other text or clocks that cannot be represented using `DigitalClock`, `PartText` is the container for text-based rendering.

entries.title: Represent the time
entries.summary: The primary job of a watch face is to show the time, and the Watch Face Format lets you create both analog and digital clocks using the [`AnalogClock`](https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/wff/clock/analog-clock) and [`DigitalClock`](https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/wff/c…

entries.title: Dynamically change element appearance
entries.summary: You may want to change the appearance of parts of the watch face, for example, change the position, size, visibility, often in response to [input data sources](https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/wff/common/attributes/source-type) such as the time of day or the accelerometer.

entries.title: Dynamically change element content
entries.summary: While `Transform` lets you change the appearance of elements or groups of elements, there might be occasions where you want to switch between a list of behaviors based on some condition. This is analogous to a `switch` statement or `if...else` statement in other languages.

entries.title: Create animated images
entries.summary: In addition to static images on the watch face, animated images can bring a further dimension to the user experience.

entries.title: Weather data in the Watch Face Format
entries.summary: Since version 2, the Watch Face Format includes support for weather data. This data covers a range of metrics and timeframes, from the current conditions to hourly and daily forecasts.

entries.title: Memory usage (anonymous RSS + swap)
entries.summary: Memory usage (anonymous RSS + swap) is a metric in Android vitals that reflects your app's memory usage.

entries.title: Interact with other apps
entries.summary: An Android app typically has several [activities](https://developer.android.com/guide/components/activities). Each activity displays a user interface that lets the user perform a specific task, such as viewing a map or taking a photo. To take the user from one activity to another, your app must use…

entries.title: Let other apps start your activity
entries.summary: If your app can perform an action that might be useful to another app, prepare it to respond to action requests by specifying the appropriate intent filter in your activity.

entries.title: Save data in a local database using Room
entries.summary: Part of [Android Jetpack](https://developer.android.com/jetpack).

entries.title: Access data using Room DAOs
entries.summary: When you use the Room persistence library to store your app's data, you interact with the stored data by defining *data access objects*, or DAOs. Each DAO includes functions that offer abstract access to your app's database. At compile time, Room automatically generates implementations of the DAOs t…

entries.title: Write asynchronous DAO queries
entries.summary: To prevent queries from blocking the UI, Room doesn't support database access on the main thread. This restriction means you must make your [DAO queries](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/room/accessing-data) asynchronous. The Room library includes integrations with several framewo…

entries.title: Create views into a database
entries.summary: The [Room persistence library](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/room) supports [SQLite database views](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_createview.html), which let you encapsulate a query in a class. Room refers to these query-backed classes as *views* , and you can use them as data ob…

entries.title: Define data using Room entities
entries.summary: When you use the [Room persistence library](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/room) to store your app's data, you define entities to represent the objects that you want to store. Each entity corresponds to a table in the associated Room database, and each instance of an entity repr…

entries.title: Migrate your Room database
entries.summary: As you add and change features in your app, you need to modify your Room entity classes and underlying database tables to reflect these changes. It's important to preserve user data that is already in the on-device database when an app update changes the database schema.

entries.title: Migrate from Room 2.x to Room 3.0
entries.summary: Room 3.0 is a major version update that transitions the library to be Kotlin-first. It supports Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP), requires Kotlin Symbol Processing (KSP), and enforces coroutines for asynchronous operations.

entries.title: Prepopulate your Room database
entries.summary: If you want your app to start with a database that's already loaded with a specific set of data, you can prepopulate the database. In Room, you can use APIs to prepopulate a database at initialization with contents from a prepackaged database file in the device's file system.

entries.title: Referencing complex data using Room
entries.summary: Room can convert primitive and boxed types, but doesn't allow object references between entities. Learn how to use type converters and why Room doesn't support object references.

entries.title: Choose relationship types between objects
entries.summary: Because SQLite is a relational database, you can define relationships between entities. But while most object-relational mapping libraries let entity objects reference each other, Room explicitly forbids this. To learn about the technical reasoning behind this decision, see [Understand why Room does…

entries.title: Define and query many-to-many relationships
entries.summary: A *many-to-many relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to zero or more instances of the child entity, and the reverse is also true.

entries.title: Define and query nested relationships
entries.summary: Sometimes, you might need to query a set of three or more tables that are all related to each other. In that case, you define *nested relationships* between the tables.

entries.title: Define and query one-to-many relationships
entries.summary: A *one-to-many relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to zero or more instances of the child entity, but each instance of the child entity can only correspond to exactly one instance of the parent entity.

entries.title: Define and query one-to-one relationships
entries.summary: A *one-to-one relationship* between two entities is a relationship where each instance of the parent entity corresponds to exactly one instance of the child entity, and the reverse is also true.

entries.title: Glance interoperability

entries.summary: Users expect apps to load fast and be responsive. An app with a slow start time doesn't meet this expectation and can disappoint users. This sort of poor experience can cause a user to rate your app poorly on the Play store or even abandon your app altogether.
